clinicalPearls: Typically bilateral, symmetric, painless and progressive visual loss with a centrocaecal scotoma and dyschromatopsia, closely overlapping the nutritional form.
Frequent offenders include ethambutol, methanol, amiodarone, prolonged linezolid, isoniazid, disulfiram, tobacco and heavy metals such as lead and thallium.
Ethambutol toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent, is often reversible if detected early, and mandates baseline and periodic monitoring of acuity and colour vision.
Methanol poisoning causes acute severe loss with disc oedema and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and may be permanent or fatal.
The papillomacular bundle is preferentially affected, producing temporal disc pallor as atrophy develops.
A meticulous drug, occupational and social history is essential, and removal of the offending agent is the mainstay of management.
Pupillary responses are relatively spared and a relative afferent pupillary defect is minimal when the process is symmetric.
Coexisting nutritional deficiency frequently aggravates toxic injury and should be sought and corrected.
reference.pathophysiology: Most toxins injure the optic nerve by impairing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and generating oxidative stress within the metabolically demanding papillomacular bundle. Ethambutol chelates copper and iron and interferes with metal-dependent respiratory chain enzymes, while the methanol metabolite formic acid directly inhibits cytochrome c oxidase. The energy failure preferentially damages small central fibres, accounting for the characteristic central and centrocaecal field defects and eventual temporal atrophy.
additionalInvestigations: Detailed medication, occupational and toxin exposure history
Colour vision testing and automated perimetry
Optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Magnetic resonance imaging to exclude a compressive lesion
Serum or urine toxicology and heavy-metal levels where indicated
Arterial blood gas and osmolar gap in suspected methanol poisoning
Vitamin B12 and folate to exclude a coexisting nutritional cause
redFlags: Acute severe visual loss with metabolic acidosis indicating a methanol emergency
Rapidly progressive loss or systemic signs of toxicity
No recovery despite withdrawal of the suspected agent
Asymmetry or focal neurological signs suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Many cases, particularly ethambutol-related, improve after early withdrawal of the offending agent, whereas methanol poisoning frequently causes permanent, severe loss. Chronic unrecognised exposure results in irreversible optic atrophy.
pitfalls: Continuing the offending drug because of inadequate monitoring, as with ethambutol
Failing to recognise methanol toxicity as a treatable emergency
Ignoring a concurrent nutritional deficiency that worsens the injury
Omitting baseline visual assessment before commencing a known optic-toxic agent
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course, Neuro-Ophthalmology
management: Prompt identification and withdrawal of the offending agent such as ethambutol, linezolid, or amiodarone is the mainstay
In methanol poisoning, urgent inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole or ethanol, correction of acidosis with sodium bicarbonate, folinic acid, and haemodialysis to clear formate
Baseline and periodic monitoring of visual acuity and colour vision in patients on potentially toxic drugs such as ethambutol
Nutritional support with B-complex vitamins and folate where a coexisting nutritional deficiency contributes
Counsel on avoidance of contributory toxins including tobacco and alcohol
Refer to neuro-ophthalmology with low-vision rehabilitation for established visual loss
